title: JPMorgan Stock Rises as Bank Lifts S&P Target to 8,000 - TradingView
content: JPMorgan Chase JPM, the largest U.S. bank by assets, raised its 2026 year-end S&P 500 target to 8,000 from 7,800. That sounds like another bullish Wall Street call. Look closer. The real story is earnings. The new target offers roughly 3.1% upside from Friday's 7,757.64 close, but JPMorgan is not counting on investors suddenly paying much richer prices for stocks. It thinks corporate profits can keep climbingand AI is becoming a bigger reason why. The numbers tell the story. JPMorgan lifted its 2026 S&P 500 earnings forecast to $365 per share from $350 and its 2027 estimate to $420 from $390. Microsoft MSFT, Amazon AMZN and Alphabet GOOG are central to the thesis. Their accelerating cloud businesses, swelling backlogs and improving cash-flow visibility suggest the mountains of money pouring into AI infrastructure are finally starting to produce something investors can measure. Earnings season is adding fuel: roughly 85.1% of the 436 S&P 500 companies that had reported through Friday beat expectations. And the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (SPY) chart shows just how American this wager remains. As of March 31, roughly $637 billion, or 97.8% of the geographic exposure shown, sat in the United States. Ireland was a distant second at 1.4%, with Switzerland, Singapore, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands and other markets barely registering. Buy SPY, and you are overwhelmingly betting on the U.S. profit machine. Here is the part that matters. JPMorgan raised its 2026 earnings estimate by roughly 4.3% and its 2027 forecast by about 7.7%, yet kept its forward valuation assumption near 20 times earnings. Translation: the market cannot simply get more expensive and call it a day. Earnings have to carry the next leg. That makes the 8,000 target both bullish and demanding. AI spending needs to turn into real profits. Margins need to hold. Inflation cannot reignite badly enough to keep rates higher for longer. Geopolitical shocks cannot derail the earnings machine. The S&P 500 is already expensive, so there is less room for excuses. The path to 8,000 is there. Now corporate America has to earn it. Select market data provided by ICE Data Services. title: JP Morgan banker who led Infantino’s Fifa sell-off has Epstein ties exposed - The Telegraph
content: Emails sent to paedophile financier include birthday greetings four years after his conviction of procuring a minor for prostitution Sam Wallace has been chief football writer since 2015, and covers all aspects of the game: its politics, its finance, transfers and sackings as well the action on the pitch itself. Previously he was the chief football writer of The Independent for 11 years. His awards include football journalist of the year, scoop of the year and the Press Awards' sports journalist of the year. He has covered six World Cups and six European Championships. You can find him on X @SamWallaceTel. Previously he was the chief football writer of The Independent for 11 years. His awards include football journalist of the year, scoop of the year and the Press Awards' sports journalist of the year. He has covered six World Cups and six European Championships. You can find him on X @SamWallaceTel. The JP Morgan Chase banker who was one of the secret figures behind the Fifa sell-off plan is also under pressure for her links to the late paedophile and financier Jeffrey Epstein. Mary Erdoes, 58, the head of the asset and wealth management division, led the bank’s efforts to find investors prepared to take part of the 20 per cent stake in Fifa which its president Gianni Infantino sought to sell. Erdoes has also come under scrutiny for her previous longstanding connection to Epstein, who died in 2019. Documents released by the US authorities indicate that Erdoes only ended JP Morgan’s relationship with Epstein in 2013, five years after he was convicted in Florida of procuring a minor for prostitution. Emails exchanged between the pair, first reported by The Banker financial news site, suggest that they were in contact regarding banking. Erdoes emailed Epstein birthday greetings from her JP Morgan account in 2012. The pair were in indirect contact via staff about the banking arrangements for another associate of Epstein, Kathryn Ruemmler, the former Goldman Sachs executive. Erdoes is, according to the New York Times, understood to be one of the few individuals who knew about Infantino’s plans as they were formulated. Those involved selling a 20 per cent stake in Fifa at a value of $4.2bn (£3.1bn) to investors led by Joshua Kushner – the brother of US president Donald Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner – and others. Infantino did not reveal the plan to his closest staff until days before the World Cup final. Joshua Kushner’s investment vehicle, Thrive Eternal, and Fifa planned to use JP Morgan to find fellow investors for the putative sale, which was subsequently abandoned by Infantino. The Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) project caused uproar in world football and has left Infantino fighting for his future as Fifa president. The European governing body, Uefa, as well as counterparts in Asia and North and Central America have threatened to break away. Erdoes, the bank’s second-highest earner last year on $32m (£24m), has not commented on her links to Infantino. The connection between the pair is not clear, although Infantino has been on stage with Erdoes when he spoke at a staff meeting at the bank. Previously JP Morgan apologised for its role in financing the 2021 European Super League. It is yet to make any comment on its role in FFE, or the relationship between Erdoes, the bank and Infantino. In terms of Erdoes’s dealings with Epstein, JP Morgan told The Banker: “We regret any association we had with the man [Epstein], but did not help him commit his heinous crimes. “The firm filed multiple Suspicious Activity Reports beginning in 2002 but heard nothing back from the government. “Mary Erdoes made the decision to close his accounts in 2013, six years before his arrest. Mary has always held herself and her colleagues to the highest standards of integrity and trust, is consistently recognised as one of the top executives in financial services and continues to be a critically important leader of our firm.” Meanwhile, Fifa will face a further embarrassing episode on Wednesday when Omar Artan – the Somali referee refused entry to the United States for the World Cup – will take charge of Uefa’s curtain-raising Super Cup. Artan has spoken about the “very tough period” he faced when denied entry to the US at Miami International Airport in June, before what should have been the highlight of his career. Tensions were already high between Fifa and Uefa before the start of the World Cup, in which Infantino attracted further scrutiny for his role in the decision to suspend the two-match ban given to United States striker Folarin Balogun. In what was a thinly veiled move to humiliate the global governing body, Artan was named the match referee for Wednesday’s Super Cup in Salzburg between Aston Villa and Paris St-Germain. Artan said on Monday: “It was a very tough period. A lot of people have sympathy for me, because when someone has been working a lot of years and is supposed to do something, and then can’t do it, it’s very challenging. “I really appreciate the support I received throughout the world, though; I’m so grateful.” Artan, 34, was subjected to an 11-hour immigration interview before he was denied entry to the US. Somalia is one of the 12 countries on the United States travel-ban list. Infantino later admitted publicly that he was powerless to overrule the ruling from Donald Trump’s administration. The Fifa president told critics at a press conference before the World Cup to “chill and relax” about the controversy, and added: “We work on everything, we try to resolve everything, [but] immediately screaming and shouting, that’s the opposite of finding a solution.” Aleksander Ceferin, the Uefa president, reacted by appointing Artan for the Super Cup, where he will become the first African official to take charge of the European season opener. Artan added: “When we got this call it was, for me and my family, really a very, very happy moment. There’s a big Somali community in Europe and in Austria, and they are over the moon with me officiating a match like this.”

title: JPMorgan just bumped its S&P 500 price target as it sees AI capex finally delivering for companies - Business Insider
content:
Returns on AI capex have been a looming question for Wall Street investors, but JPMorgan says that elusive AI monetization is a big reason it's boosting its S&P 500 price target for the year. The bank's strategists hiked their target for the benchmark index on Monday, as they eye an "increasingly visible" payoff from the huge sums of money being poured into the AI buildout. In a note to clients, a team led by the bank's Dubravko Lakos-Bujas raised their year-end forecast for the benchmark index to 8,000, a slight increase from the bank's prior year-end target of 7,800 and about 3% higher than Monday's levels. Strategists cited higher earnings as investors finally begin to see the ROI from the billions spent in AI capex — a key concern that has weighed on hyperscaler stocks all year. It's been a rough few months for the tech trade, with investors intermittently punishing large AI spenders as concerns build over valuations and whether all that capex will be worth it. The Roundhill Magnificent Seven ETF, for instance, is down 2% from its peak in May. Meta, one of the biggest spenders of the Mag Seven group, is down 7% year-to-date. But the outlook for many of these firms has already started to improve during the second quarter, JPMorgan said. Strategists pointed to expanding backlogs, improved cash flow visibility, and stronger growth in cloud businesses, which have allowed firms like Google, Amazon, and Microsoft to clear "a high investor expectation bar," they wrote in a note. "This suggests that monetization may start ramping faster than spending, which should support stronger future revenue growth and further alleviate concerns about ROIC," the bank said. Take a smarter break in your day - and see how far you get. AI capex is expected to keep rising. The bank said consensus estimates now forecast total capex to reach around $900 billion by the end of the year, up about 85% from last year. The figure could rise to $1.2 trillion by the end of 2027, JPMorgan estimated. Corporate earnings growth, meanwhile, shows no sign of slowing down. Of the S&P 500 firms that have already reported their results for the second quarter, 86% have beaten on earnings, and 76% have beaten on revenue estimates, according to the latest update from FactSet. The index is also on track for the highest blended earnings growth rate in five years, the analytics firm said on Friday. Despite the bullish outlook, strategists pointed to several risks that still hang over the market. Free cash flow at most of the hyperscalers will likely continue to be negative through 2027, JPM said. The US economy also remains K-shaped from a consumer perspective, the bank added, referring to the growing bifurcation between top earnings and lower- to middle-income Americans, who remain pressured by the cumulative impact of inflation. JPMorgan Chase (NYSE:JPM) is providing its Kinexys multi chain tokenisation system as the blockchain infrastructure for a new tokenised US dollar money market fund share class launched by Schroders. Schroders is the first global asset manager to receive approval for a tokenised share class in a US dollar money market fund using J.P. Morgan's blockchain platform. The launch marks a move from internal testing to real client deployment for J.P. Morgan's blockchain business, with regulatory approval in place. The project is presented as a step toward greater efficiency and automation in institutional fund flows that run through J.P. Morgan's digital infrastructure. This kind of progress in bank grade blockchain and digital infrastructure is part of a wider shift in how markets are wiring up for data heavy applications, and that broader theme is where many investors are now focusing attention 56 AI infrastructure stocks JPMorgan Chase sits at the center of global capital markets, and its stock has drawn attention from investors watching the link between traditional banking and blockchain infrastructure. The shares most recently closed at $357.52, with returns of 9.8% year to date and 25.8% over the past year. Many readers now view this blockchain activity as part of the broader story around JPMorgan Chase and its role in institutional fund flows. Beyond the headline: 1 risk and 3 things going right for JPMorgan Chase that every investor should see. The JPMorgan Chase Narrative centers on using new financial technologies to deepen its role in global payments, wealth and asset management. This Schroders launch sits right on that bet, because it turns Kinexys from internal plumbing into infrastructure that outside asset managers now rely on. "Ongoing investment and active participation in tokenization, stablecoins, and payment innovations ... positions JPMorgan to benefit competitively from the next wave of technology adoption in banking and payments..." Read the full JPMorgan Chase narrative to see the case behind these numbers On the bull side, Schroders choosing Kinexys for a live, regulated US dollar money market fund is direct evidence that JPMorgan Chase can sell its blockchain stack into institutional fund flows. That aligns with the Narrative's focus on higher fee revenue from payments and asset management, and with recent wins such as Dukhan Bank going live on the same network. It also reinforces JPMorgan's position against large peers such as Citigroup and Bank of America that are building their own digital rails. The bear case is not invalidated. Tokenised funds still face regulatory complexity, and success here does not automatically resolve concerns around fintech competition or commoditised payment pricing that analysts have flagged. If tokenisation becomes crowded with specialist platforms, JPMorgan Chase may have to share economics or invest heavily to keep Kinexys attractive for clients such as Schroders. Overall, this news leans slightly toward the bullish Narrative. It turns the story of "ongoing investment" in tokenisation into a concrete product that external institutions are now using in production, while still leaving open questions about how broad and profitable that market becomes. content: The S&P 500 and Nasdaq are holding small gains Monday but the Dow is lower and the tape is not broad. Friday’s payrolls miss sent stocks to record levels on the expectation that the Fed would have a harder time hiking in September. Monday is testing that bet. WTI crude is near $80 after Iran issued new demands on the Strait of Hormuz and the 10-year Treasury yield climbed back to 4.68% after touching 4.60% on Friday’s jobs data. The S&P 500 is trading on the strong side of its minor pivot and both trends remain up on the swing chart. But the split between growth holding gains and the Dow sitting lower tells you this rally has not widened yet. Wednesday’s CPI decides whether it does. At 14:33 GMT, the Dow Jones Industrial Average was at 53,988.71, down 48.22 points or 0.09%. The S&P 500 was trading at 7,769.06, up 11.42 points or 0.15%. The Nasdaq Composite was at 26,716.58, up 25.97 points or 0.10%. The S&P 500 Index is edging higher shortly after the opening on Monday. Early in the session, the market crossed to the strong side of a minor pivot at 7,745.92, giving it a little upside momentum. Trader reaction to this pivot should set the tone today. A sustained move over 7,745.92 will indicate the presence of buyers. If upside momentum begins to build, then look for a test of the record high at 7,793.68. A move through this level will reaffirm the minor and main trends. A sustained move under the pivot will signal the presence of sellers. Taking out the minor bottom at 7,698.15 will change the minor trend to down. This will also shift momentum to the downside. The first major support is the former top at 7,620.90. Buyers may return to defend this level since old tops can become new bottoms. A failure to hold this level will indicate the selling pressure is increasing. This could lead to a 50% to 61.8% correction of the rally from 7,313.92 to 7,793.68. These targets are 7,553.80 to 7,497.19, respectively. Additionally, the 50-day moving average at 7,497.50 forms a support cluster with the 61.8% level. Although the trend is up, some traders feel the steep nature of the five-day rally has created an overvalued situation. This makes the market vulnerable to a near-term correction. The first sign that this correction is starting will be a trade through the 7,698.15 minor bottom. Crude is doing more damage. WTI is near $80 after Iran issued new demands before reopening the Strait of Hormuz to shipping traffic. The market is putting supply risk back into the oil price and that feeds straight into inflation expectations. The jobs report weakened the labor side of the Fed’s case for September. Oil climbing back toward last month’s levels can rebuild the inflation side in a hurry. The 10-year yield rose to 4.68% from 4.65% at Friday’s close. That is not a large move but it shows the bond market is not treating one weak payrolls print as the final word on the Fed. Friday’s rate relief trade sent growth stocks higher and pushed yields to 4.60%. The bond market has already taken half of that move back. Wednesday’s CPI is the number. PPI Thursday and retail sales Friday follow. The June reports landed before Hormuz disruptions hit energy costs. This round of data carries those disruptions and the market will see it immediately. A soft print and Friday’s rally keeps running. A hot one with WTI near $80 and the same buyers who chased growth stocks Friday start selling Wednesday afternoon. The payrolls miss does not disappear but it stops being enough on its own. J.P. Morgan lifted its year-end S&P 500 target to 8,000 from 7,800 Monday. The 2026 EPS forecast went to $365 from $350 and the 2027 number to $420 from $390. Google, Amazon and Microsoft did the heavy lifting on that call. Their results convinced the firm that AI spending is showing up in revenue, not just costs. The numbers back it up. Of 436 S&P 500 companies through Friday, 85.1% beat estimates. The long-term average is 68%. J.P. Morgan still capped the target at 20 times forward earnings. Rates are not coming down, Hormuz is not resolved and the market is absorbing heavy equity and debt supply. The multiple reflects what is working against stocks, not just what is working for them. SpaceX touched $135 in the opening minutes before pulling back to $134, up about 1%. That $135 is the IPO price and the level the market is watching. The stock has bounced more than 20% off last week’s record low and Friday’s lockup expiry passed without the selling wave traders feared. A hold above the IPO price and buyers are back in control. A rejection and $120.56 is the first downside target. Meta picked up about 1% on Zuckerberg’s comments about keeping AI models broadly accessible. The stock is still part of the AI leadership group but the spending has to start showing up in revenue before the market gives it credit for the vision. Berkshire Hathaway gained about 2% after posting strong earnings. Greg Abel is signaling he will put the cash pile to work through buybacks and equity investments. The Dow needed something besides technology to participate Monday and Berkshire gave it a reason. Monday’s gains are narrow. The S&P 500 is near its record. The Nasdaq is positive. The Dow is not participating. Oil near $80 and the 10-year yield climbing back from Friday’s lows are the two forces working against the rate relief trade that produced last week’s rally. CPI Wednesday is the week. Soft inflation keeps the repricing intact and growth stocks keep running. Hot inflation with crude climbing on Hormuz gives the Fed its argument back. The minor pivot at 7,745.92 is holding. A break below 7,698.15 starts the correction and the 50-day cluster near 7,497 is where it finds support. AI investment is driving U.S. data center construction at a scale that demands new approaches to financing. J.P. Morgan's Investment Banking teams break down how corporate debt, project-level debt and multi-layered equity structures are being deployed — and what risks developers and investors need to manage. The U.S. data center market is experiencing unprecedented growth, fueled by the rapid adoption of AI, cloud computing and enterprise migration. In 2026 alone, J.P. Morgan estimates capex for hyperscalers — large—scale cloud and technology companies — will reach $697 billion. As John Servidea, global co-head of Investment Grade Finance at J.P. Morgan, said, “AI financing is the biggest secular theme in our professional lifetimes.” The industry ambition is visible in recent transactions. Project Stargate, the AI infrastructure initiative announced by the U.S. government in January 2025, plans to invest up to $500 billion in U.S. data centers and energy infrastructure over four years. J.P. Morgan originated $9.6 billion across two construction loans for the initiative’s Abilene, Texas campus, acting as lead left, sole underwriter and sole structuring agent on both transactions — a single engagement that illustrates the scale of capital now moving into AI infrastructure. “AI financing is the biggest secular theme in our professional lifetimes.” Global co-head of Investment Grade Finance, J.P. Morgan Behind every AI model training run and cloud query sits a physical support structure: purpose-built facilities that require land, power, cooling and connectivity at industrial scale. “That’s digital infrastructure. Most people don’t realize it, but there’s billions of dollars of physical assets supporting virtually every technology experience that you enjoy today,” said Scott Wilcoxen, head of Global Digital Infrastructure Investment Banking at J.P. Morgan. Historically, this infrastructure spanned foundational physical networks including cell towers, fiber-optic cables and satellites. As AI adoption and cloud computing grow, data centers are emerging as the most critical facilities to support increased demand. Not all open land can support industrial-grade utilities and long-term expansion possibilities. Developers must closely evaluate data center build sites based on unique requirements, including: Acreage: According to IBM, the average onsite data center typically has between 2,000 and 5,000 servers, with a footprint reaching 100,000 square feet — roughly the equivalent of 38 standard tennis courts. Connection: The space must offer proximity to power transmission and fiber networks, or the project must consider installation of these connections as part of the build cost. Environmental security: Consideration of earthquakes, floods and other environmental risks is critical to ensure consistent compute capabilities with minimal interruptions. Community considerations: Developers must address concerns from communities near data center build sites prior to breaking ground. This goes beyond paperwork to include public hearings and stakeholder negotiation. Doing so is a crucial step in establishing permitting rights across zoning, building permits, water rights and more. “Data doesn’t move in a vacuum, it moves over a medium.” Head of Global Digital Infrastructure Investment Banking, J.P. Morgan AI infrastructure financing requires both scale and bespoke structuring. The capital needs are large, build timelines are long, and the cash flow profile often differs from what traditional investment-grade markets are accustomed to underwriting. “What’s particularly exciting for us is the level of creativity that is required to finance all of this. Thinking about how to raise this capital in the most efficient way requires a lot of collaboration across teams and markets,” said Servidea. In AI infrastructure, debt most often comes in two core structures: corporate (balance-sheet) debt and project-level debt. Corporate debt allows for speed and flexibility: proceeds can fund capex across data center buildouts, power-related spending, networking and compute without tying the lender to one specific project’s performance. Project-level debt, by contrast, is underwritten primarily to a defined set of project cash flows, often supported by long-term contracts or otherwise high-visibility revenues. The trade-off is less flexibility and more structural complexity, in exchange for tighter lender protections and debt sizing that is anchored to the asset’s own cash generation. The June 2026 financing of Hut 8’s Beacon Point data center in Nueces County, Texas illustrates how project-level debt can be structured around durable, contracted cash flows. J.P. Morgan acted as lead left bookrunner on the $4.25 billion senior secured notes offering, which was 100% pre-leased under a 15-year triple-net lease to a high investment-grade tenant. The transaction achieved a 95% loan-to-cost ratio — the highest ever for a high-performance computing data center bond — and priced at T+165, the tightest spread ever recorded for a data center construction bond. Equity is the risk-absorbing capital in AI infrastructure, used to fund growth and shoulder uncertainties that debt investors typically discount, such as technology obsolescence, ramp-up timing, utilization volatility and customer concentration. In practice, equity is often used to get projects built and scaled, with the expectation that the business can later add more debt once revenues are contracted and performance is more predictable. As capital needs grow, equity financing structures have become increasingly complex, often drawing on multiple layers of the capital stack simultaneously. “More often, forming this capital means going to multiple pockets, across multiple regions and, in many instances, looking across multiple layers of the capital stack and incorporating both structured as well as common equity to ultimately fund these investments,” said Wilcoxen. CoreWeave’s April 2026 capital raise demonstrates how AI-first companies are increasingly drawing on multiple layers of the capital stack simultaneously. J.P. Morgan acted as lead left and active bookrunner on a $5.25 billion combined offering comprising of $1.75 billion in senior unsecured notes and $3.5 billion in convertible senior notes. This deal represents one of the largest combined high-yield and convertible offerings ever executed. It also reflects both the scale of capital required to build and operate AI infrastructure at speed and the sophistication of the financing structures now available across the sector. “Investors are not blindly buying everything. There’s a tremendous amount of capital being deployed, but investors are taking the time to do the credit work, understand the stories and figure out relative value and pricing. To me, that’s a healthy sign for the market.” Global co-head of Investment Grade Finance, J.P. Morgan As the demand for data center capacity grows, pressure builds on key components of the supply chain. According to Wilcoxen, the most crucial of these is power supply. Demand for compute is rising faster than many regional grids can support, and the friction shows up in aging transmission infrastructure, limited local capacity and multiyear wait times to connect to power that can push project timelines out materially. As a result, time to power has become a limiting factor for data center and compute deployments. “Accelerating time to power is a top priority for many of our clients, but the grid infrastructure isn’t there,” said Wilcoxen. “There’s a lot of work to do.” Beyond the grid itself, the supply chain is constrained by natural resources and physical inputs that are harder to scale quickly than capital. Builders must secure available land in the right locations, water access and cooling requirements, and appropriate permitting that determines whether a project can move from plan to energized facility. Clients are responding by securing sites and utility pathways sooner, evaluating alternative cooling approaches where feasible and bringing energy and infrastructure specialists into the diligence process to underwrite power availability and execution risk with the same rigor as the underlying compute demand. Over-building is a parallel risk: AI capital expenditure has, in many cases, outpaced monetization. “The uncertainty around how, when and in what magnitude end-user demand materializes in a monetizable way does make it difficult to plan out over a multiple-year cycle,” said Wilcoxen. As a result, long lead times for power and construction are colliding with rapidly evolving technology cycles and shifting customer needs. In response, many operators and sponsors are trying to structure buildouts in phases, pursue more contracted or pre-committed demand where possible, and maintain optionality so capacity can scale with real adoption. Debt concentration is an emerging systemic consideration as AI’s share of the overall financing market grows rapidly. “I don’t think we’re at a point yet where concentration limits are a huge concern, but it is part of the dialogue because as a portion of the overall market, AI is growing very quickly,” said Servidea. Practically, clients are working to keep funding channels resilient by diversifying capital sources, matching debt structures to cash-flow visibility and avoiding overly correlated exposures to a single counterparty, technology node or demand narrative. The throughline is that the next phase of AI infrastructure buildout will be shaped as much by execution discipline as by the availability of capital. “We’re building the physical underpinnings of the future technological progress of mankind.” Head of Global Digital Infrastructure Investment Banking, J.P. Morgan Investor appetite for AI infrastructure is strong, but it’s not indiscriminate. “Investors are not blindly buying everything. There’s a tremendous amount of capital being deployed, but investors are taking the time to do the credit work, understand the stories and figure out relative value and pricing. To me, that’s a healthy sign for the market,” said Servidea. Rather than jumping on the bandwagon, investors are positioning themselves to finance a long-term buildout, considering downside protection as much as upside. “The red lights would start flashing if it felt like there was blind euphoria. That’s not what we’re seeing,” Servidea said. While AI is a major incremental driver, infrastructure buildout is broader than a single theme. “This entire AI dynamic is additive to an already extraordinarily large investment base,” said Wilcoxen. For instance, public cloud and software-as-a-service (SaaS) models are expected to expand meaningfully in the near future. Compute growth won’t map one-to-one with revenue or usage because efficiencies improve over time, but the direction of travel remains clear: more workloads, more data movement and more always-on digital services will translate into continued expansion of data centers, networks and supporting hardware. The next phase of AI infrastructure will reward platforms that can secure reliable, scalable power, navigate grid access and interconnection timelines, and structure financing around durable demand signals. If AI meaningfully reshapes products and workflows, the practical implication is sustained investment not just in compute, but in the physical and energy foundations that make that compute usable at scale. “When you think about all the different things society will be able to do with AI over the next five years, 10 years, 20 years, it’s really hard to comprehend what that’s going to ultimately require,” said Wilcoxen. “We’re building the physical underpinnings of the future technological progress of mankind.” The data center surge: Building the backbone of the digital age Our experts dive deep into the world of digital infrastructure — exploring the critical role of data centers, fiber, and towers in powering today’s digital economy. They also discuss the risks of overbuilding, and the importance of operational expertise. AI is transforming global economies and revolutionizing industries.  delivered quarterly results that moved past what market watchers had been penciling in, with the lift concentrated squarely in trading desks and dealmaking and underwriting work rather than spread evenly across every corner of the franchise NYSE Composite. The beat arrived alongside a broader wave of strength among large domestic lenders, many of which also cleared their respective bars this earnings season as capital-markets activity picked up and deal pipelines grew noticeably healthier. Taken together, the results paint a picture of a banking group finding sturdier footing after a stretch of choppier conditions, with dealmaking desks and trading floors doing much of the heavy lifting. Heading into this stretch of quarterly reporting, expectations around large domestic banks had grown cautiously constructive rather than exuberant. Market watchers had been weighing a shifting rate environment against steadier loan demand, and there was a general sense that net interest margins would remain roughly stable even as attention pivoted toward fee-generating businesses like trading and underwriting. That backdrop set a relatively modest bar, which made it easier for the largest lenders to clear expectations when brisk trading conditions and a livelier calendar of corporate transactions materialized. The mood entering the reporting period also reflected a broader normalization in capital-markets conditions after a stretch where corporate issuance and merger activity had been comparatively subdued. Trading desks, in particular, had been benefiting from elevated volatility in rates and currency markets, which tends to widen the pool of institutional activity flowing through the largest banks. That dynamic gave several lenders a tailwind even before individual quarterly figures were released. Perhaps most notably, the earnings season reinforced a theme that had been building for a while: the largest, most diversified banks are proving better positioned to absorb shifting rate expectations than smaller, more narrowly focused institutions. Diversified fee revenue, healthy trading engines, and improving deal pipelines gave the biggest names a cushion that many regional peers simply do not have. JPMorgan Chase operates across a sprawling set of businesses that span everyday consumer banking, commercial lending, asset and wealth management, and a large-scale corporate and markets arm. That breadth has long been described as one of the defining features of the franchise, since strength in one segment can offset softness elsewhere during any given stretch. In the most recent reporting period, it was the corporate and markets arm that carried much of the weight, with trading desks across equities, bonds, and currencies posting brisk activity levels. Consumer-facing operations, meanwhile, continued to show a steady, if unspectacular, pattern, with card spending and deposit trends tracking largely in line with recent quarters. Commercial banking also displayed a generally stable posture, with loan demand from mid-sized and larger corporate clients described as measured rather than surging. Asset and wealth management arms continued to benefit from broader stability in markets, which tends to support fee-based revenue streams tied to assets under management. What stood out this period was less about any single business line and more about the balance across the franchise. Even as some segments delivered only modest contributions, the scale of the trading and dealmaking engines was enough to lift the overall results meaningfully above where market watchers had positioned themselves. Capital-markets activity across the banking group has clearly shifted into a more constructive gear. Underwriting desks have been busier, corporate issuance has picked up, and merger and transaction pipelines across several large banks have grown noticeably healthier than in prior stretches. That combination of brisker trading and a fuller dealmaking calendar has become one of the defining threads of this earnings season, touching nearly every large lender that reported results. Alongside that capital-markets rebound, there has been growing public commentary about inflationary pressure tied to heavy corporate spending on artificial intelligence infrastructure. Large companies across industries have been funneling meaningful sums into data centers, computing capacity, and related buildout, and that spending pattern has become a talking point among bankers who see it feeding into broader price pressures across the economy. Banks, in turn, have been engaging more heavily with corporate clients on how to adopt AI tools broadly across their own operations, from back-office processing to client-facing services. That heavier engagement between large banks and their corporate clients on AI adoption is beginning to show up in advisory conversations as well, with dealmakers increasingly fielding questions about how artificial intelligence buildout might reshape corporate spending patterns, capital allocation, and longer-term operating structures. Banks with the largest advisory and underwriting franchises appear best positioned to capture that conversation, since corporate clients tend to lean on established relationships when navigating unfamiliar territory. A more favorable regulatory backdrop has become one of the more consistently cited themes across the banking group this reporting season. Expectations around a lighter-touch regulatory stance have encouraged some banks to lean more aggressively into capital-markets activity, trading, and underwriting, businesses that tend to be sensitive to how much flexibility institutions feel they have. That dynamic has been described as a meaningful tailwind for the largest, most capital-markets-heavy franchises in particular. Credit quality across the banking group has generally remained sound, with delinquency and charge-off trends described in largely stable terms rather than showing signs of meaningful deterioration. That stability matters because it gives banks room to lean into growth-oriented activity, such as trading and dealmaking, without needing to set aside disproportionately larger reserves against souring loans. A steady credit backdrop has therefore been cited as one of the quieter but more important supports underpinning this earnings season. The capital-markets cycle itself appears to be turning more constructive after a stretch of comparatively subdued issuance and transaction activity. Corporate clients seem more willing to pursue transactions, tap debt and equity markets, and pursue strategic combinations, a shift that tends to benefit the largest banks disproportionately given their scale in underwriting and advisory work. If that cycle continues to build, it could extend the tailwind that showed up so clearly in this round of quarterly results. One of the more notable threads running through JPMorgan Chase's recent operational moves has been an expanding set of partnerships with financial technology platforms in the payments space. Rather than building every capability internally, the bank has been leaning into collaborative arrangements that pair its scale and balance sheet strength with the speed and specialization that smaller technology-focused platforms can offer. That approach reflects a broader industry pattern in which large, established banks increasingly work alongside nimble fintech players rather than treating them purely as rivals. Payments has become one of the more competitive corners of financial services, with merchants, corporate treasurers, and consumers all pushing for faster, more seamless transaction experiences. By deepening ties with fintech platforms, JPMorgan Chase appears to be positioning its payments business to keep pace with shifting client expectations without sacrificing the security and scale advantages that come with operating one of the largest banking franchises in the country. This sector-wide push toward payments partnerships also dovetails with the broader theme of AI adoption inside banking. Many of the fintech platforms that large banks are partnering with bring embedded automation and AI-driven tools directly into payments workflows, which in turn helps large banks modernize client-facing services more quickly than if they attempted every build in-house. Few institutions in the domestic banking group can match the sheer scale and diversification that JPMorgan Chase brings to its operations. That combination allows the franchise to absorb softness in any single business line without it derailing overall results, a dynamic that played out clearly in the most recent quarter, when strength in trading and dealmaking more than offset a comparatively subdued period for other segments. Diversification also gives the franchise flexibility to lean into whichever part of the cycle happens to be most constructive at a given moment. When capital-markets activity is brisk, as it has been recently, the corporate and markets arm can carry a larger share of the load. When consumer spending or lending trends strengthen instead, other parts of the franchise can step forward. That rotation of strength across business lines is a structural advantage that fewer, more narrowly focused competitors can replicate. Scale also matters when it comes to technology spending, regulatory compliance, and the kind of large-scale infrastructure buildout that increasingly defines competitive positioning across banking. Being among the largest players in the domestic banking group gives JPMorgan Chase meaningful room to fund ambitious technology initiatives while still delivering solid quarterly results, a balance that smaller institutions often find harder to strike. The headline story of the reporting period was straightforward: JPMorgan Chase posted results that narrowly topped what had been broadly expected, with the outperformance traced almost entirely back to dealmaking, underwriting, and trading. Fee generation from underwriting and advisory work climbed noticeably, reflecting a fuller pipeline of corporate transactions moving through the system, while trading desks benefited from elevated activity levels across rates, currencies, and equities markets. Within the financial stocks category, the results were seen as one of the stronger examples of how brisk capital-markets conditions can lift overall performance even when other segments deliver a more muted contribution. What made the beat particularly notable was its breadth across the wider banking group rather than being isolated to a single institution. Several other large domestic lenders also topped expectations during the same stretch, reinforcing the sense that the strength tied to capital-markets activity, deal pipelines, and stable credit conditions was a sector-wide phenomenon rather than a company-specific story. That pattern tends to draw broader attention to the group as a whole, since it signals that the tailwinds supporting results are structural rather than isolated. Market reaction to the results has been measured rather than dramatic. Options-market sentiment around the shares has been described as mixed in recent sessions, with modest upward moves showing up on comparatively light trading days rather than any single, sharp repricing. That pattern indicates market participants are still digesting how durable the current capital-markets tailwind might prove to be, even as the underlying quarterly figures themselves cleared expectations comfortably. Technology spending has become an increasingly central part of how large banks describe their operating priorities, and JPMorgan Chase is no exception. The franchise has continued to describe artificial intelligence tools as a meaningful area of internal focus, spanning everything from fraud detection and back-office automation to client-facing tools designed to speed up service and reduce friction across everyday banking interactions. That technology push is closely tied to the broader industry conversation about AI-driven inflationary pressure. As corporate clients across sectors ramp up their own spending on computing infrastructure and AI tooling, banks are finding themselves drawn deeper into advisory conversations about how to finance, structure, and manage that buildout. JPMorgan Chase's scale gives it a natural seat at that table, since large corporate clients often prefer working with banks that have already built out meaningful internal AI capabilities of their own. Beyond client-facing applications, technology spending also touches core infrastructure, cybersecurity, and the kind of resilient, always-on systems that large banking franchises are expected to maintain. That ongoing spending represents a meaningful, if less headline-grabbing, part of how the bank allocates resources each period, and it is increasingly framed as a long-term operational priority rather than a discretionary expense. Even with a broadly constructive earnings season behind it, the banking group continues to navigate a handful of persistent challenges. Chief among them is the inflationary pressure tied to heavy corporate spending on AI infrastructure, a theme that has drawn increasing public commentary from bankers who worry that surging demand for computing capacity, energy, and specialized labor could feed into broader price pressures across the economy. That dynamic complicates the already uncertain path for interest rates, since sustained inflationary pressure tends to influence how quickly monetary authorities feel comfortable adjusting their stance. Rate uncertainty remains a live theme as well. While net interest margins have generally remained stable across the banking group, any meaningful shift in the rate environment, in either direction, carries implications for lending margins, deposit costs, and overall earnings composition. Banks with more diversified fee revenue, including trading and dealmaking, tend to be somewhat better insulated from swings tied purely to rate movements than institutions more heavily reliant on traditional lending margins. Competitive pressure also continues to intensify, both from within the traditional banking group and from fintech platforms encroaching on payments, lending, and wealth management territory. That competitive backdrop is part of what has pushed large banks like JPMorgan Chase toward deeper partnerships with financial technology platforms rather than treating every new entrant purely as a rival. Navigating that blend of cooperation and competition has become a defining challenge for large, diversified banking franchises heading into the coming periods. Within the broader group of large domestic banks, JPMorgan Chase continues to stand out for its combination of scale, diversification, and consistency across cycles. While several other major lenders also posted quarterly results that topped expectations this season, the breadth of JPMorgan Chase's franchise, spanning consumer banking, commercial lending, asset and wealth management, and a large-scale corporate and markets arm, gives it a structural advantage when it comes to weathering uneven conditions across individual business lines. Other large banks have leaned more heavily on specific strengths, whether that means a particularly robust trading desk, a strong regional commercial lending presence, or a deep wealth management franchise. JPMorgan Chase's advantage lies less in dominating any single category and more in maintaining meaningful strength across nearly every category simultaneously, which tends to smooth out results across changing market conditions. That comparative positioning has become especially relevant this earnings season, given how broadly the sector-wide themes, brisk capital-markets activity, healthier deal pipelines, stable credit conditions, and deregulation tailwinds, have lifted large banks collectively. In that environment, the institutions with the widest and deepest set of business lines tend to capture the most benefit, since they are exposed to virtually every corner of the improving backdrop simultaneously rather than just one or two segments. Large bank shares carry outsized relevance for the broader market given their heavy representation within major indices, including the S&P 500. When a sizable group of large domestic lenders collectively tops expectations during a single earnings stretch, the ripple effects tend to extend well beyond the banking group itself, since financial shares often serve as a barometer for broader economic conditions, credit availability, and capital-markets health. The current stretch of broadly constructive banking results, paired with themes like deregulation tailwinds, rising domestic capital expenditure trends, and a more active capital-markets cycle, has helped support a generally steadier tone across financial shares within major benchmarks. That steadier tone matters for a wide range of market participants, since financial institutions sit at the center of how capital flows through the broader economy, from corporate lending to underwriting to everyday consumer banking services. Given how central large banks are to overall market composition, continued strength or weakness within the group tends to carry meaningful signal value for broader sentiment. As the current earnings season winds down, attention is likely to remain fixed on whether the brisk capital-markets activity, stable credit conditions, and improving deal pipelines that defined this stretch can be sustained into the periods ahead. title: Memory chip supply crunch will last 2 more years, JPMorgan warns - Yahoo Finance Singapore
content: Tip: Try a valid symbol or a specific company name for relevant results The AI-driven memory chip crisis has a ways to go before its status is downgraded to business as usual. JPMorgan strategist Jay Kwon is making a double bullish call on the entire memory space. First, Kwon thinks the memory chip crisis is far from over. "Higher memory total addressable market driven by both pricing and volume, S-D shortage continues for the next two years," Kwon wrote in a note on Monday. "Memory demand broadening out from GPU to CPU appears to have been underestimated by investors (conceptually well known but actual S-D impact underlooked) and remains a key source of potential upward revisions to demand." Second, with the crisis rolling on, Kwon thinks the summer swoon in memory stocks has ended. "3Q26 will likely be an expectation reset quarter, but we remain bullish on memory," he wrote. "After a strong four quarters of outperformance over the overall AI ecosystem, memory shares experienced a 25% correction in 3Q26 to date largely due to a peak-out sentiment amidst: a) series of near-term EPS expectation misses; b) slower-than-expected CSP AI capex spending; and c) mainstream memory content optimization. We acknowledge that the road to a valuation re-rating will take time relative to upward EPS revisions, driven by share appreciation; however, we see strong upside to memory stock prices trading at earnings and P/E valuation metric on a smoothening earnings trajectory from LTA and a higher shareholder return profile." Kwon is bullish on Korean memory stocks — Micron (MU) in the US, Kioxia (KI5.F) in Japan, and Winbond (2344.TW) in Taiwan. Micron shares have exploded 202% this year compared to a 13% advance for the S&P 500 (^GSPC), per Yahoo Finance AlphaSpace data. The stock has corrected this summer, however, dropping 10% in the past month on overvaluation fears. The CEO of memory chip play Sandisk (SNDK) perhaps put it best on his earnings call last week about the state of the market. "We spent a lot of time over the last two or three quarters really working very deeply with our largest customers on committing demand," Sandisk CEO David Goeckeler said. "We have over four years of visibility now. We feel very good about where the franchise is." That's a lot of business visibility, largely because the memory crisis is unlikely to abate anytime soon. It may even last longer than JPMorgan's call expects. For a while now, the story has been can all the massive investment on AI pay off for tech firms - especially big tech? The major worry is that the massive outlay in terms of capital expenditure on AI would grow too big, with returns not being able to catch up. Alphabet (Google) kicked off the earnings season in playing to that narrative, recording its first ever quarter with negative free cash flow as a public company. But come the end, other tech firms took that as a learning lesson and told investors what they needed to hear. That being capital expenditure on AI is under control and that the money will come through. And JP Morgan is pointing to exactly that as carrying the AI trade to its next leg higher from here. The firm notes that: "As elevated backlogs convert into recognised revenue, cloud growth should remain well supported, helping validate rising AI capex, strengthen order coverage, and further ease ROIC (return on invested capital) concerns." Adding that the benefits of rising AI investment were much clearer in Q2 this year, especially among the likes of Amazon and Microsoft which saw strong cloud growth, larger backlogs, and better cash-flow visibility. All of which JP Morgan says should further ease any major worries about the massive spending that is still ongoing. That is leading the firm to revise higher their year-end forecast for the S&P 500 to 8,000 now. However, they are maintaining the forward valuation multiple target at about 20 times in citing geopolitical risks and higher interest rates among key potential headwinds for the market. That being said, their bullish call more or less extends to next year with JP Morgan seeing EPS for 2026 at $365 (previously $350) and $420 for 2027 (previously $390). Basically, after spending quite a few years being a founder by myself and being also a corporate, I thought that I want to come back to be an entrepreneur, but in a different capacity to set up my own fund to confound OTP venture and to start working with founders and supporting the founders. We focus on disruptive technologies. We focus on visionary founders doing really difficult tech. And we are particularly focused on three areas space and dual use and novel computing, NII, as well as robotics and physical AI. We are looking for unique ideas and good geographic focus. But by far the most important thing is the the most important criteria is a unique founder founder that can take the company from zero to a great success, and desire just a handful of great personalities that can actually make it happen. In OTB ventures. We are big believers of the sector of European resilience. We want to play an important role in it. We want to support startups and founders, building next generation European resilience companies and hopefully contribute to this trend over the next years. We don't want to take the backseat. We don't want to be a background noise. We want to be an active investor. We understand our role. We are not the founders. The founders are at the driving seat, but we are here to support them and we are here to understand what their needs are, how we can potentially help them with growing their business, but also sometimes being an alter ego and being just a partner that can share experience and hopefully make together the success. We won't make a success without founder making a success. JP Morgan is probably not only the largest financing institution in the world, but it's also an organization that understands very well business from different perspective, from the founders perspective, from the corporate perspective, from the deal perspective. Being an entrepreneur, is having the vision and energy to move the mountains. The satisfaction, the energy that comes together, is just impossible to replicate. And it's close to nothing else that I can think of. And this is something that really excites me, and I hope to be doing this for the rest of my life. An entrepreneur at heart, Adam Newinski understands what it takes to grow a successful business. Now, as co-founder of OTB Ventures, he invests in some of the most ambitious tech startups in Europe. We talk to him about his journey, what the role of a founder means—and what it’s like to switch from building businesses to backing them. It was over 25 years ago, in the latter days of the dotcom bubble, that Adam Newinski cofounded his first tech business in what was then a relatively unknown sector called fintech. It would prove to be a turbulent period. Despite the sector facing increasing pressure as the bubble began to burst, the company managed to evolve. Shortly after, Adam achieved a successful exit from the business. By this time, he knew he had a strong appetite for entrepreneurship and continued to look for emerging opportunities. “I also co-founded a consumer bank in Ukraine with a friend of mine, so I’ve spent quite some time really understanding what it’s like to be a founder,” he recalls. “I then spent 16 years in banking…but I’ve always thought of myself as an entrepreneur first.” Despite a fruitful career, Adam soon found the pull of enterprise impossible to ignore. “I thought I wanted to come back to be an entrepreneur, but in a slightly different capacity.” The result was OTB Ventures, which Adam co-founded in 2017. It allowed him to put his enterprising mindset to renewed use in support of European founders tackling technically ambitious ventures. Rather than broadly investing across software, the VC firm concentrates on what Adam calls “deep tech”; businesses built around difficult scientific or engineering innovations with long development cycles. “We focus on early-stage investments in disruptive technologies, and on visionary founders doing really difficult tech. We are particularly concentrated on three areas: space and dual use, GenAI and novel computing and robotics and physical AI.” For Adam, though, this is about more than investing, his approach has grown from his own experiences and philosophy. “OTB Ventures doesn’t want to take a backseat or become background noise. We want to be an active investor. We understand our role—the founders are at the driving seat—and we are here to support them and understand what their needs are. “Sometimes being a partner that can share experiences and advice can make all the difference.” Supporting founders is clearly central to the way OTB Ventures approaches opportunities, but every investment must start with the same question: who is worth backing? “We look for unique ideas and good geographic focus, but by far the most important factor is someone that can take the company from zero to a great success.” “I love [working with] founders who have a relatively strong opinion but open to discussion—and want to understand what other people have to say, then draw their own conclusions.” While founders and leadership undoubtedly help to shape every investment decision, Adam is as equally passionate about the technologies these companies are building and the future opportunities they offer. “We are big believers in the security resilience sector. And it’s a great time for Europe to focus on AI, space, dual use, robotics—even semiconductors. These are the topics that Europe has been strengthening for the last 18 months, and it needs to continue. We want to play an important part in it.” It is certainly a sector that has become increasingly relevant as the world shifts towards fragmentation and technology grows ever more sophisticated. But for Adam, the key to unlocking a startup’s potential is still to focus on the founders. “It’s important to have disruptive tech. But by far the most important [assets] are the founders.” Supporting emerging economies and founders is a philosophy that resonates with our own values. As Adam explains, it’s often the people behind the business that ultimately determine its success. “J.P. Morgan is not only the largest financing institution in the world, it’s also an organisation that understands business from different perspectives; both the founders and the corporate.” We look forward to continuing our partnership with Adam into the future as he works with companies at the very forefront of technology across Europe, and to collaborate with other innovative founders and entrepreneurs across the world. Letting founders stay in the “driving seat” while still being an active, helpful partner—and picking the right founder, since the person matters most in taking a company from “zero to a great success,” especially in deep tech with long cycles. Firsthand founder experience: understanding what founders need, sharing practical advice, and supporting tough decision-making without taking over. You move from executing decisions to enabling others—listening more, advising when useful, and thinking long-term around disruptive deep-tech innovation. After building and exiting a fintech startup, co-founding a bank in Ukraine, and spending years in banking, he returned to entrepreneurship “in a slightly different capacity” by co-founding OTB Ventures in 2017 to back European deep-tech founders. title: JP Morgan reckons Rolls-Royce shares are worth £18! - Yahoo Finance UK
content: Tip: Try a valid symbol or a specific company name for relevant results Rolls-Royce Holdings' (LSE:RR.) shares received a significant boost on 30 July, when the group reported its half-year results and announced another increase in its profit and cash forecasts. I say 'another' because, since the group released its 2023 numbers, it's raised its earnings guidance nine times. Now, it's upgraded its underlying operating profit forecast to £4.7bn-£4.9bn. In February, it was predicting £4bn-£4.2bn. This is a big increase. In fact, JP Morgan was so impressed it lifted its December 2027 price target to £18. Previously, it was £16.25. In addition, its future (2026-2030) earnings per share forecasts have been raised by 13%-19%. Why is the investment bank so optimistic about the prospects of the UK's fourth most-valuable listed company? Rolls-Royce has three operating businesses and, during the first half of the year, each of them performed strongly. In terms of underlying operating profit, they all recorded very healthy double-digit growth when compared to the first six months of 2025: And there could be more to come. At 30 June, the group had orders for 2,266 large engines. The backlog for its defence business was equivalent to three times annual revenue and, in power systems, its half-year order intake was 50% higher than for the same period a year ago. Indeed, it's this strong group-wide performance that lies behind JP Morgan's enthusiasm: In our view, this was arguably the most impressive of the nine beats for two reasons. First, it is much harder to beat off a high base than a low base. Second, all three divisions significantly beat expectations and now have a higher earnings outlook. And the investment bank isn't the only one impressed by Rolls-Royce's latest numbers. Jefferies described the first-half performance as "exceptional". Other investors appear excited too. No wonder the stock's climbed 11% since results day ( to 8 August). However, it always pays to be cautious. The group's shares aren't cheap. This means any sign of a slowdown and its market-cap could tumble sharply. It's undeniable that repeatedly beating earnings forecasts over a sustained period becomes increasingly difficult.
